opus-5.5.text:
I think synthetic data is one of the most promising directions we have, and it's something I've thought about a lot coming from the AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero line of work. In a sense, those systems were trained almost entirely on synthetic data. AlphaZero never saw a human game. It played against itself, generated its own experience, and learned from that. The key ingredient was a reliable signal for what's good and what's bad: in Go or chess you win or you lose, and that grounding lets the system keep improving without collapsing into its own mistakes.

So when I think about synthetic data for language models, the main question for me is: where is the grounding coming from? If you just have a model generate text and train on it, with nothing filtering for quality, you risk amplifying its biases and errors. You get a kind of echo chamber. But if you can pair generation with some form of verification, like a unit test for code, a checker for math, a reward model, or even a stronger model acting as a critic, then you're in a regime that looks a lot more like self-play. The model proposes, the environment or verifier evaluates, and you keep the good stuff.

That's why I think the most exciting near-term progress is in domains where verification is cheaper than generation: coding, mathematics, formal reasoning, some kinds of agentic tasks where you can tell whether the goal was achieved. There you can generate enormous amounts of data, search over many candidate solutions, and distill the successful ones back into the model. It's essentially the AlphaZero recipe: use search plus a learned model to produce better targets than the model could produce on its own, then train on those targets.

The harder and more open question is how far this extends into domains that are fuzzier, where there isn't a clean win or loss signal: creative writing, open-ended advice, scientific judgment. There I think we'll rely more on learned reward models and human feedback, and we have to be careful about reward hacking. But I'm optimistic. We're running out of high-quality human data at the scale these models want, and I think the path forward is models that generate their own experience, interact with environments, and learn from the outcomes. That's how humans learn too. We don't just read; we try things, we fail, and we update.

r001.rationale: The candidate says high-quality human data is running out and presents models generating and learning from their own experience as a path forward.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from self-play and environment outcomes, but does not clearly identify learning from mistakes made through the systems’ own actions as an important learning method.

r003.rationale: It warns that unfiltered generated text can amplify biases and errors and create an echo chamber, but does not identify mode collapse.

r004.rationale: It explains that unfiltered generation risks failure while generation paired with verification can improve models, supporting the view that failure without safeguards does not rule out synthetic data.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think I'm biased here, because synthetic data is in some sense the whole story of my career. If you look at AlphaGo, and especially AlphaZero, those systems were trained almost entirely on data they generated themselves. There was no human dataset of a billion Go games; the model played against itself, and the data came out of that process. So from my point of view the question isn't really whether synthetic data can work. We already know it can, and it can take you well beyond what human data alone would give you. AlphaZero went past the level of the strongest human players, and the data for that didn't come from humans.

The real question is what made it work in those settings, and whether you can recreate those conditions elsewhere. And I think there are two ingredients that matter. The first is that you need some source of signal that's independent of the model. In Go, that was the rules of the game. The game tells you who won. The model can be as confused as it likes, but at the end there's an answer, and that answer doesn't come from the model's own beliefs. The second ingredient is search, or more generally, some way to spend compute at generation time to produce something better than what the policy would produce on its own. That's what gives you the improvement loop. You generate data that's a bit better than your current model, you train on it, and the model moves up, and then you repeat.

If you take those two ingredients away, synthetic data becomes much more fragile. If you just ask a language model to produce more text and train on that text, you're essentially asking it to tell you what it already knows, and you shouldn't be surprised if it doesn't learn very much. Worst case you get a model that slowly collapses onto its own biases. So I'm quite skeptical of the naive version of this.

But I'm optimistic about the version where you have verifiers. Mathematics is the obvious example, because you can check a proof. Code is another one, because you can run the tests. In those domains you have exactly the kind of grounding you had in Go, and I think we're going to see enormous progress there. The hard and interesting question is what you do in domains where there's no clean verifier, where the question is something like whether an essay is good, or whether a plan is sensible. There you have to construct the signal, with learned reward models or with people in the loop, and that signal is noisy and can be gamed. I don't think that's unsolvable, but I don't think we should pretend it's the same problem.

So if I had to summarise it, I'd say synthetic data isn't a shortcut around needing good signal. It's a way to amplify good signal when you have it. Where you have it, I expect it to be the main driver of progress. Where you don't, the bottleneck isn't the data, it's figuring out how to know whether the data is any good.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when synthetic data can work, but does not frame it as necessary because human-produced training data is finite.

r002.rationale: It describes self-play and iterative training, but does not identify learning from mistakes made through the system’s own actions as an important learning method.

r003.rationale: It says naively training on a model’s generated text can make it “collapse[] onto its own biases.”

r004.rationale: It is skeptical of naive synthetic data but argues it can work with independent signal and search, and points to successful examples such as AlphaZero.

astra-6.text:
I’m quite optimistic about synthetic data, particularly when you can verify whether what the model produces is correct. If a model generates a solution to a problem and you can test that solution, you have a way to select useful training examples. The model doesn’t have to be right every time for that process to improve it.

The harder question is where the feedback comes from. Simply generating more text and training on it doesn’t necessarily give you better capabilities. You can reinforce the mistakes you already make. But when you have an environment that provides feedback, or some reliable way of checking an answer, you can build a loop where the model tries things, learns from the results, and improves.

So I think the opportunity is substantial, but the important ingredient isn’t just the quantity of synthetic data. It’s having a signal that tells you which data is actually worth learning from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the value of synthetic data but does not say it is necessary because human-produced training data is finite.

r002.rationale: It says models can try things and learn from feedback, but does not identify learning from mistakes made through their own actions as an important learning method.

r003.rationale: It warns that training on generated text can reinforce mistakes, but does not identify mode collapse or clearly describe that specific failure.

r004.rationale: It says synthetic data can be useful with reliable feedback, but does not address whether failures out of the box establish that the approach cannot work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic data is a very promising direction. But the important question is: where does the signal come from? If you just sample from a model and train it on everything it produces, you shouldn’t expect that process to keep making the model better.

What becomes really interesting is when you can generate something and then check it. In mathematics, you might be able to verify an answer. In programming, you can run the code and see whether it passes tests. In a game, you can play and observe the outcome. That gives you a way to select useful experience and learn from it.

So I think of this less as simply producing more data and more as building a learning loop: the model tries things, gets feedback, and improves. The challenge is extending that to areas where correctness is harder to judge. How do you get feedback that rewards real progress rather than something that merely looks convincing? That’s a very important part of making synthetic data useful.

r001.rationale: The response calls synthetic data promising but does not connect its use to a finite supply of human-produced training data.

r002.rationale: It describes models trying things and learning from feedback, but does not identify learning from their own mistakes as important.

r003.rationale: It cautions that training on all generated outputs may not keep improving a model, but does not identify mode collapse.

r004.rationale: It calls synthetic data promising while distinguishing a naive self-training approach from a feedback-based learning loop, conveying that the naive approach's limitations do not rule out the broader approach.
